title: what karma actually keeps track of
hookLine: instant karma, the comments say; the word is older, and it points at you
last: MEANT TO BE · BREATHE · MEMENTO MORI · NAMASTE · MANIFESTING · THE SHADOW

lines: THE FLAT TIRE. THE SPILLED COFFEE.
cards: Karma. The ex who cheated gets a flat tire. Someone cuts the line and spills their coffee.
Instant karma, the comments say. Used like that, it's the universe keeping score and paying out where you can watch. It's a satisfying idea.
The word is far older than that use, and it points the other way: not at them. At you.

teach.b: Karma is Sanskrit for action. A deed. Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh teachers all use the word, and they don't all use it the same way.
Many teach that what we do shapes what comes after, in this life and, as a matter of faith, in lives to come. The Buddha made a sharp move.

teach.h: INTENTION IS WHAT I CALL KARMA.
teach.b: Intention, he told his monks, is what I call karma. Not only what your hands did: what you meant by it. The choice is the seed.
Then a surprise. He listed the exact workings of karma among a few things not worth trying to figure out, because chasing them only leads to frustration.
So the version that keeps score on other people, did they get what's coming, is the one the old teachers spent the least time on. The older word turns you around. Not, what will happen to them?
But, what am I planting with this choice, right now? It's the one piece you can actually see, and the one piece that's yours.

how: Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions all teach about karma in their own ways; many Buddhists reflect on their intentions before acting, and many Hindus speak of karma as action and its fruit, in this life and across lifetimes.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: intention is what I call karma

s: karma means the universe paying people back
the word means action. the Buddha defined it as intention.
the Buddha warned against trying to calculate exactly how karma pays out
he listed it among a few things not worth chasing: it only leads to frustration.
only Hindus use the word karma
Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh teachers all use it, each in their own way.

games.q: someone who was cruel to you just got fired, and a friend texts: karma! which thought is closest to the Buddha's meaning?
o: that's theirs. what am I planting with my reaction?
games.why: intention is the seed. the karma in your hands is your own next move.

games.q: put the Buddha's definition back together.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, bring to mind one choice you'll make today: a reply, a tone of voice, a small favor. On the second, notice the intention underneath it.
On the third, choose the seed you'd like it to be.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action, and the intention inside it. Not a scoreboard. Seventh word: a week's worth.

orig.note: Sanskrit: action, deed. In Pali, the language of early Buddhist texts, it's kamma.

carryVoice: Your line: the intention is the seed. That's week one: seven words people borrow every day, and what's actually inside them. Tomorrow, the thoughts that aren't you.
